EXPOSÉ IV
The cohomology class associated with a cycleby A. Grothendieck, written by P. Deligne

This exposé is inspired by notes of Grothendieck, which formed a preliminary version of [21]. In it one defines the cohomology class of a cycle \(X\) in a separated, smooth scheme of finite type over a field, and one proves that intersection corresponds to the cup-product.

Chapter 1 contains some general sorites. In Chapter 2, one defines the class of a cycle, in several situations more general than the one mentioned above. The main compatibility not considered is that between the direct image of a cycle and the trace morphism in cohomology. In Chapter 3, one deduces from this formalism the Lefschetz trace formula for an endomorphism with isolated fixed points of a proper and smooth scheme over an algebraically closed field \(k\) – and for a Frobenius endomorphism of a curve.
We make the following conventions:

1. “scheme” means noetherian separated scheme (this is largely a hypothesis of convenience).

  2. In Chapter 2, one fixes an integer \(n\), and \(n\) is invertible on all the schemes considered.

  3. In Chapter 3, one fixes a prime number \(\ell\), and \(\ell\) is invertible on all the schemes considered. The cohomology used is always \(\ell\)-adic cohomology:

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X) = \mathbb{Q}_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n) \text{.} \]
Cohomology classes of cycles, trace morphisms, … are defined by passage to the limit from the case of finite coefficients \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\) (cf. [21]).
1 Cohomology with supports and cup-products
This section contains reminders of general topology, which the reader is invited to consult only as the need arises.
1.1 \(H^1\) and torsors

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be an abelian sheaf on a site \(X\). It is known that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) classifies the \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsors on \(X\). We shall normalize (\(=\)choose the sign of) the isomorphism \((\)set of isomorphism classes of \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsors\()\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) in such a way that for every exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathscr{G}\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathscr{H}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) and every \(h\in\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{H})\), the \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsor \(\beta^{-1}(h)\subset \mathscr{G}\), on which \(\mathscr{F}\) acts by \((f,x)\mapsto \alpha(f)+x\), is of class \(\partial h\).

Let \(\mathscr{P}\) be an \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsor. If \((U_i)\) is an open covering of \(X\), and \(p_i\) a section of \(\mathscr{P}\) over \(U_i\), one associates with \(\mathscr{P}\) the Čech cocycle
\[ p_{i j} = p_j - p_i \qquad \text{(} p_{i j}\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(U_i\times U_j,\mathscr{F}) \text{).} \]

If, according to the usual rule, one defines the map \(\operatorname{\check H}^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})\) in such a way that it is a morphism of \(\delta\)-functors, the image of \((p_{i j})\in \operatorname{\check H}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) is the class of \(\mathscr{P}\), as normalized by 1.1.1.

The definition of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})\) is the following: for \(\mathscr{F}^\bullet\) a resolution of \(\mathscr{F}\) with acyclic components, \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\Gamma(X,\mathscr{F}^\bullet)\). The \(\delta\)-functor structure is obtained by associating with a short exact sequence of sheaves a short exact sequence of resolutions that remains exact after applying the functor \(\Gamma\). If \(\mathscr{F}^\bullet\) is a resolution of \(\mathscr{F}\), the connecting homomorphism \(\partial\) associated with
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathscr{F}^0 \ar[r]^-d & \ker(d) \ar[r] & 0 } \]
induces the opposite of the defining isomorphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F}) = \Gamma\left(X,\ker(d)\right)/d \Gamma(X,\mathscr{F}^0)\).

Let \(U\) be an open subset of \(X\) (a subsheaf of the final sheaf) and let \(D\) be the “complementary closed set.” It is known that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) classifies the \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsors on \(X\) trivialized over \(U\). For every short exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\xrightarrow{\alpha} \mathscr{G}\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathscr{H}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\), and every section with support in \(D\) \(h\in\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^0(X,\mathscr{H})\), the torsor \(\beta^{-1}(h)\), trivialized over \(U\) by the section \(0\), has class \(\partial h\).
The long exact sequence of cohomology with supports

\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(U,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r]^-\partial & \cdots } \]
is defined from the sequence of functors
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \Gamma_D \ar[r] & \Gamma \ar[r] & \Gamma(U,-) \ar[r] & 0 } \]

(exact on injective sheaves). For every section \(f\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(U,\mathscr{F})\), \(\partial f\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) is the class of the trivial torsor \(\mathscr{F}\), trivialized over \(U\) by the section \(f\).
Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\). If \(\mathscr{F}\) injects into \(j_* j^* \mathscr{F}\), the exact sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & j_* j^* \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & j_* j^* \mathscr{F} / \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & 0 } \]

yields \(\partial:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(j_* j^*\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^0(j_* j^* \mathscr{F}/\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^1(X,\mathscr{F})\). The composite map

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(U,\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,j_* j^*\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,j_* j^*\mathscr{F} / \mathscr{F}) \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^1(X,\mathscr{F}) } \]
is the opposite of the map considered in 1.1.4.

Recall that if \(\mathscr{L}\) is an invertible sheaf on a scheme \(X\), the corresponding \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor is the sheaf \(\operatorname{Isom}(\mathscr{O},\mathscr{L})\), on which \(\mathbb{G}_m\) acts by \((\lambda,f)\mapsto f\circ (\lambda\cdot) = \lambda f\). Recall also that if \(D\) is a Cartier divisor on \(X\), and \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) the inclusion of the complementary open set, the invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{O}(D)\) is the subsheaf of \(j_*\mathscr{O}_U\) consisting of the local sections \(s\) such that \(s f\) lies in \(\mathscr{O}_X\), for \(f\) a local equation of \(D\).
1.2 Cup-products

In this subsection, we develop some remarks on the cup-products in cohomology with supports which will be of use to us again, in [Duality], to relate Poincaré duality of curves and self-duality of the Jacobian.

Let \(X\) be a site, \(Y\) a closed subset of \(X\), and \(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G}\) two abelian sheaves on \(X\). For example: \(X\) a scheme, \(Y\) a closed subscheme and \(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G}\) sheaves on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\). Let us define a product
\[ \tag{1.2.1.1} \Gamma_Y(X,\mathscr{F})\otimes \Gamma(Y,\mathscr{G}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \Gamma_Y(X,\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathscr{G}) \text{.} \]

The product of a section \(s\), with support in \(Y\), of \(\mathscr{F}\) by a section \(t\) of \(\mathscr{G}\) over \(Y\) is obtained as follows: locally on \(X\), \(t\) is the restriction to \(Y\) of a section \(t'\) of \(\mathscr{G}\) over \(X\), and one forms the product \(s\otimes t'\). It has support in \(Y\), and does not depend on the choice of \(t'\), which legitimizes the definition and makes it possible to globalize it.
Let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the inclusion morphism. The local analogue of (1.2.1.1) is the product.
\[ \tag{1.2.1.2} i^!\mathscr{F}\otimes i^*\mathscr{G} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} i^!(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathscr{G}) \text{,} \]
from which (1.2.1.1) is deduced by applying \(\Gamma(Y,-)\).

Let us derive these arrows. Let \(\mathscr{K}\), \(\mathscr{L}\) and \(\mathscr{M}\) be in the derived category, and a bilinear map \(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathscr{L}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{M}\). By deriving (1.2.1.1), one deduces

\[ \tag{1.2.2.1} \mathsf{R}\Gamma_Y(X,\mathscr{K}) \overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,\mathscr{L}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma_Y(X,\mathscr{M}) \]
inducing

\[ \tag{1.2.2.2} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^i(X,\mathscr{K})\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^j(Y,\mathscr{L}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{i+j}(X,\mathscr{M}) \]
(the cup-product). The local arrow (1.2.1.2) yields
\[ \tag{1.2.2.3} \mathsf{R} i^! \mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} i^*\mathscr{L} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} i^!\mathscr{M} \text{,} \]
from which (1.2.2.1) is deduced by applying \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,-)\).

Above, I have passed over in silence the conflicts entailed by the use, in one and the same formula, of right derivations (\(\mathsf{R}\Gamma\)) and left derivations (\(\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\)).

1. In the next subsection, the right derived functors considered will all be of finite cohomological dimension. This makes it possible to work systematically in the derived categories \(\mathsf{D}^-\). In order to have complexes that are both flat and flasque, one uses the canonical flasque resolutions as in [2].

  2. For a more general theory, it ceases to be possible to interpret the bilinear maps of \(\mathscr{K}\) and \(\mathscr{L}\) into \(\mathscr{M}\) as morphisms from \(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathscr{L}\) into \(\mathscr{M}\). For example, \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_Y(X,\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,\mathscr{L})\) is not defined if the two factors are in \(\mathsf{D}^+\). One solution is to work in \(\mathsf{D}^+\), to define

    \[ \operatorname{Bil}(\mathscr{K},\mathscr{L};\mathscr{M}) = \varinjlim \hom(\mathscr{K}'\otimes\mathscr{L}',\mathscr{M}') \text{,} \]

    where the limit is taken over the quasi-isomorphisms \(\mathscr{K}'\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{K}\), \(\mathscr{L}'\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{L}\), \(\mathscr{M}\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{M}'\) (\(\mathscr{K}'\), \(\mathscr{L}'\), \(\mathscr{M}'\) bounded below) and where \(\hom\) stands for “morphism of complexes, up to homotopy,” and to use systematically such bilinear maps, without ever mentioning any \(\otimes\).
1.2.4 Second theme

Let \(U\) be an open set of \(X\) and \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) the inclusion morphism. For \(\mathscr{K}\) in the derived category, on \(U\), one sets \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(U,\mathscr{K})=\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,j_!\mathscr{K})\). For \(\mathscr{K}\), \(\mathscr{L}\) and \(\mathscr{M}\) on \(U\), and a bilinear map \(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathscr{L}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{M}\), one wants to define

\[ \tag{1.2.4.1} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(U,\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(U,\mathscr{L})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(U,\mathscr{M}) \text{.} \]

At the level of sheaves, and of their global sections, such a product is deduced from the isomorphism \(j_*\mathscr{F}\otimes j_!\mathscr{G}\xleftarrow{\sim} j_!(\mathscr{F}\otimes \mathscr{G})\), but one must be careful of the fact that \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!\) is in general not the derived functor of the functor \(\Gamma(X,j_!-)\).
One begins by defining
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R} j_* \mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} j_! \mathscr{L} & j_!(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{L}) \ar[r] \ar[l]_-\sim& j_!\mathscr{M} . } \]
Applying \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,-)\), one finds

\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(U,\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(U,\mathscr{L}) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathsf{R} j_*\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,j_!\mathscr{L}) \ar[r] & \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,j_! \mathscr{M}) . } \]
Here again, the conflict between left and right will be resolved in the next subsection by working in \(\mathsf{D}^-\).

Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be an open subset and \(i:Y\hookrightarrow U\) a closed subset of \(U\). Let \(\overline{Y}\) be a closed set of \(X\) such that \(\overline{Y}\cap U=Y\), (for example, the complement of \(U\setminus Y\)). Let \(\mathscr{K}\) be on \(U\). One sets \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_{Y!}(U,\mathscr{K})=\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(Y,\mathsf{R} i^!\mathscr{K})\) where \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!\) is relative to the inclusion of \(Y\) into \(\overline{Y}\). For every open set \(V\) of \(U\) containing \(Y\), \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_{Y!}(U,\mathscr{K})\) maps into \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(V,\mathscr{K})\): if one again denotes by \(i\) the inclusion of \(\overline{Y}\) into \(X\), by \(j\) that of \(Y\) into \(\overline{Y}\) and by \(k\) that of \(V\) into \(X\), one has \(\mathsf{R} i^!\mathscr{K} = j^*\mathsf{R} i^! k_!(k^*\mathscr{K})\), whence a morphism \(j_!\mathsf{R} i^!\mathscr{K} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} i^! k_!(k^*\mathscr{K})\). Applying to it \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(\overline{Y},-)\), one finds \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_{Y!}(U,\mathscr{K})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma_{\overline{Y}}(k_! k^* \mathscr{K}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(k_! k^*\mathscr{K}) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(V,\mathscr{K})\).

For \(\mathscr{K},\mathscr{L},\mathscr{M}\) on \(U\), and a bilinear map \(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathscr{L}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{M}\), one wants to define

\[ \tag{1.2.5.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(U,\mathscr{K})\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_!^m(Y,\mathscr{L}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{Y!}^{n+m}(U,\mathscr{M}) \]
(this last group itself mapping into \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_!^{n+m}(V,\mathscr{M})\)). In the derived category, one has to define

\[ \tag{1.2.5.2} \mathsf{R}\Gamma_Y(U,\mathscr{K}) \overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R}\Gamma_!(Y,\mathscr{L}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma_{Y!}(U,\mathscr{M}) \text{.} \]

One identifies \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_Y\) with \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,\mathsf{R} i^!\mathscr{K})\). The sought-for product is then of the type (1.2.4.1) relative to the local product (1.2.2.3) on \(Y\): \(\mathsf{R} i^! \mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathscr{L} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} i^! \mathscr{M}\).

Above, we have laid out the absolute formalism. There is a parallel relative version, with \(\Gamma\) replaced by \(f_*\), for \(f\) a morphism \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\).
1.3 The Koszul rule

Let \(A\) be a commutative ring, and \((V_i)_{i\in I}\) a finite family of graded \(A\)-modules (or \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-graded). Let us recall the definition of the graded tensor product \(\bigotimes_{i\in I} V_i\), in the sense of the Koszul rule (cf. [2]). For each total order \(a\) on \(I\), we shall define a module \(V(a)\). We shall also define a transitive system of isomorphisms \(\varphi_{a b}:V(b)\xrightarrow{\sim} V(a)\), and the graded tensor product of the \(V_i\) will be the “common value” \(\varprojlim V(a)\) of this system of modules. One takes

1. \(V(a) = \bigotimes_{i\in I} |V_i|\) (ordinary tensor product of the ungraded modules underlying the \(V_i\)).

  2. if the \(x_i\in V_i\) are homogeneous, one takes \(\varphi_{a b}(\otimes x_i) = (-1)^N \otimes x_i\), where \(N\) is the sum of the \(\deg(x_i)\deg(x_j)\) taken over the pairs \((i,j)\) such that \(i<_a j\) and \(i>_b j\).
Example 1

Take \(I=\{1,2\}\) and let \(a\) be the order in which \(1<2\), \(b\) the order in which \(1>2\). Let \(v_i\in V_i\) be homogeneous, and denote by \(v_1\otimes v_2\) (resp. \(v_2\otimes v_1\)) the image in the graded tensor product of the product of the \(v_i\) in \(V(a)\) (resp. \(V(b)\)). One has
\[ v_1\otimes v_2 = (-1)^{\deg(v_1)\deg(v_2)} v_2\otimes v_1 \]
(Koszul rule).
Example 2

If the \(V_i\) are all of degree \(1\), one has, relating the module underlying the graded tensor product and the ordinary tensor product of the modules \(|V_i|\) underlying the \(V_i\), a canonical isomorphism
\[ \left|\bigotimes V_i\right| \simeq \bigotimes |V_i|\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\bigwedge^{|I|}\mathbb{Z}^I \text{.} \]
Example 3

For \(A\) a field, and \(X_i\) a finite family of spaces, the Künneth formula reads \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(\prod X_i,A\right) = \bigotimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_i,A)\).
Let \(V^\vee\) be the graded dual of \(V\). The canonical map
\[ \tag{1.3.1} V^\vee\otimes V = V\otimes V^\vee \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A \]
is \(v'\otimes v\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} v'(v)\).
We now suppose that \(A\) is a field, and we consider only finite-dimensional vector spaces. The canonical isomorphism
\[ \tag{1.3.2} W\otimes V^\vee \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \hom(V,W) \]

is \(w\otimes v'\mapsto \left(v\mapsto w\cdot v'(v)\right)\). Via this isomorphism, the composition \(\hom(Y,Z)\otimes \hom(X,Y)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \hom(X,Z)\) is identified with the morphism induced by (1.3.1): \(Z\otimes Y^\vee\otimes Y\otimes X^\vee \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z\otimes X^\vee\).
The trace of \(f:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) (zero for \(f\) homogeneous of degree \(\ne 0\)) is the image of \(f\) under

\[ \tag{1.3.4} \operatorname{tr}:\hom(V,V) {\xleftarrow{\sim}}_\text{(1.3.2)} V\otimes V^\vee = V^\vee \otimes V \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}_\text{(1.3.1)} A . \]
One checks easily that, for \(f\) of degree \(0\),
\[ \tag{1.3.5} \operatorname{tr}(f,V) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(f,V^i) \text{.} \]

If one expresses that the two morphisms composed of morphisms (1.3.1) \(V^\vee\otimes V\otimes W^\vee\otimes W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k\) commute, one finds that, for \(f:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} W\) and \(g:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) homogeneous, one has
\[ \tag{1.3.6} \operatorname{tr}(f g) = (-1)^{\deg(f)\deg(g)} \operatorname{tr}(g f) \text{.} \]

blocks.html: 2 The cohomology class associated with a cycle
2.1 The class of a divisor

Let \(D\) be a Cartier divisor in a scheme \(X\). Away from \(D\), the invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{O}(D)\) is trivialized by the section \(1\). The class \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\) of \(D\), in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m)\), is the class of the corresponding \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor trivialized on \(X\setminus D\) (1.1.6 and 1.1.4).

Let \(\partial:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X\setminus D,\mathbb{G}_m)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^{i+1}(X,\mathbb{G}_m)\) be the morphism 1.1.4. If \(D\) admits a global equation \(f\), multiplication by \(f\) is an isomorphism from \(\mathscr{O}(D)\), trivialized by \(1\) on \(X\setminus D\), to \(\mathscr{O}\), trivialized by \(f\) on \(X\setminus D\). By 1.1.4, one therefore has
\[ \tag{2.1.1} \operatorname{cl}(D) = \partial f \text{.} \]

For every morphism \(u:X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) such that \(u^* D\) is again a Cartier divisor (i.e., \(u^{-1} D\) disjoint from \(\operatorname{Ass}(X')\)), one has \(\operatorname{cl}(u^* D) = u^*\operatorname{cl}(D)\). If one wanted such a functoriality for every morphism \(u\), one would have to consider not Cartier divisors, but more generally invertible sheaves equipped with a section.

Recall that the integer \(n\) is henceforth assumed invertible on the schemes considered. Let \(\partial:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^i(X,\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^{i+1}(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) be the coboundary for the Kummer exact sequence \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1.2

The class \(\operatorname{cl}_n(D)\) of \(D\) in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) is \(\partial \operatorname{cl}(D)\).
When there is no risk of confusion, one will omit the mention of \(n\).
The diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X\setminus D,\mathbb{G}_m) \ar[r]^-\partial \ar[d]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m) \ar[d]^-\partial \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X\setminus D,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) } \]

is anticommutative. If \(D\) admits a global equation \(f\), \(\operatorname{cl}_n(D)\) is therefore the opposite of the image under \(\partial\) of the class in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X\setminus D,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) of the \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\)-torsor of \(n\)-th roots of \(f\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1.4

Let \(i\) be the inclusion of \(D\) into \(X\). If \(D\) and \(X\) are regular, the cohomology sheaves with supports \(\mathsf{R}^p i^! \boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) are zero for \(p=0,1\), and \(\mathsf{R}^2 i^!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n = \underline{\mathbb{Z}/n}\), generated by \(\operatorname{cl}_n(D)\).

It suffices to prove that, for \(X\) strictly local and \(D\) defined by a regular parameter, one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^p(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = 0\) for \(p=0,1\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) generated by \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\). Denoting by \(\sim\) the reduced cohomology, one has \(\widetilde{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^{p-1}(X\setminus D,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_D^p(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\). The assertion for \(p=0,1\) expresses that \(D\) does not disconnect \(X\), and for \(p=2\) follows, via 2.1.3, from Abhyankar's lemma.

This is a partial analogue of the relative theorem ([I]Cohomologie étale, 5.3.4). Grothendieck conjectures that the \(\mathsf{R}^p i^! \boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) are zero for \(p\ne 2\), at least for \(X\) excellent (purity conjecture), but this is known only in characteristic \(0\) ([2]).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.1.5 (Fundamental compatibility)

Let \(X\) be a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(P\) a closed point of \(X\) and \(\operatorname{tr}\) the composite \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_P^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{tr}} \mathbb{Z}/n\). One has

\[ \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{cl}(P) = 1 \text{.} \]
Let \(\overline{X}\) be the projective smooth curve completing \(X\). The formula expresses that the invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{O}(P)\) on \(\overline{X}\) is of degree \(1\).
2.2 Cohomological method

Let \(X\) be a (noetherian) scheme. Recall that a subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\) is said to be a local complete intersection, of codimension \(c\), if, locally (on \(Y\)), it is defined by a regular sequence of \(c\) equations in \(X\). For \(X\) the spectrum of a local ring \(A\) with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) and \(Y\) with ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\), this means that \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(A/\mathfrak{a},A) = 0\) for \(i<\dim(\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a})=c\), and every sequence of elements of \(\mathfrak{a}\), whose image in \(\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}\) is a basis of \(\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}\), is a regular sequence of equations for \(Y\).

Let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be a local complete intersection, of codimension \(c\). We propose to define a local fundamental class \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\) that is a global section of the cohomology sheaf with supports \(\mathsf{R}^{2c}i^! \mathbb{Z}/n(c)\) (recall that \(\mathbb{Z}/n(c)=\boldsymbol{\mu}_n^{\otimes c}\)).

Locally, \(Y\) is the intersection of a sequence of \(c\) divisors \(D_i\), and one defines \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\) as the cup-product of the \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\). Each \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) has support in \(D_i\); their product has support in \(Y\). That, locally, this product does not depend on the choice of the \(D_i\) follows from 2.2.3 below and from the following invariance properties:

1. compatibility with localization;

  2. independence of the order of the \(D_i\) (the \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) are of degree \(2\), even, so the cup-product is commutative);

  3. the product depends only on the “flag” \(D_1\supset D_1\cap D_2\supset \cdots\supset Y\).
To prove c), one notes the existence of a product (variant of 1.2.1)

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{D_1}^\bullet(X)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{D_1\cap D_2}^\bullet(D_1)\otimes \cdots \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^\bullet(D_1\cap \cdots \cap D_{c-1}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^\bullet(X) \text{;} \]

the product of the \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) is again the product of the (\(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) restricted to \(D_1\cap \cdots \cap D_{i-1})=(\operatorname{cl}(D_1\cap \cdots \cap D_i)\) in \(D_1\cap \cdots \cap D_{i-1})\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2.3

Let \(A\) be a local ring with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) and \(u=(u_1,\dots,u_c)\), \(v=(v_1,\dots,v_c)\) two regular sequences generating the same ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\). Then there exists a sequence \(w_i\) (\(1\leqslant i\leqslant N\)) of such sequences, connecting them, such that \(w_{i+1}\) is deduced from \(w_i\) by a permutation, or by changing only the last element.

Since permutations are available, it would amount to the same thing to allow oneself to change a single element, rather than the last. By 2.2.1, one thus reduces to verifying that, in the vector space \(\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}\), one can pass from one basis to another by a sequence of permutations and of changes of basis modifying only a single vector. The linear group is indeed generated by the diagonal, elementary, and permutation matrices.
The same methods make it possible to define a local fundamental class for every \(Y\subset X\) locally definable by \(c\) equations (where fewer equations suffice, the class is zero).

One can pass from such a local fundamental class, in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(Y,\mathsf{R}^{2 c} i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\), to a global fundamental class, in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\), when one has semi-purity results at one's disposal:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2.6

  1. If \(\mathsf{R}^p i^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(p<2 c\), then

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(Y,\mathsf{R}^{2 c} i^! \mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \text{.} \]

  2. Let \(Z\) be a closed subset of \(Y\), with complement \(V\) in \(Y\), and \(k\) the inclusion of \(Z\) into \(X\). If \(\mathsf{R}^p i^! \mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(p\leqslant 2 c\), then

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \hookrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_V^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \text{.} \]

    If \(\mathsf{R}^p i^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(p\leqslant 2 c+1\), this arrow is an isomorphism.

The hypothesis \(\mathsf{R}^p i^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) is equivalent to \(\mathsf{R}^p i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(c)=0\). This said, (i) can be read off from the spectral sequence \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(Y,\mathsf{R}^q i^!)\Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{p+q}(X,-)\). If \(k_1\) is the inclusion of \(Z\) into \(Y\), one has \(k=i k_1\), whence \(\mathsf{R} k^! \mathbb{Z}/n=\mathsf{R} k_1^! \mathsf{R} i^!\), and the long exact cohomology sequence for \(Z\subset Y\) yields a long exact sequence

\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\left(Z,\mathsf{R} k^! \mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^i\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_V^i\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]
from which (ii) follows.
2.2.7 Amplification

Proposition 2.2.6 remains valid for \(i\) an arbitrary morphism separated of finite type, and \(2 c\) an arbitrary integer (positive or negative), provided one replaces \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\) by \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 c}\left(Y,\mathsf{R} i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\), and similarly for \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_V\).
The following semi-purity results follow from [24]. We shall recall their proof.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.2.8

Let there be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes of finite type

\[ \xymatrix{ Y \ar[r]^-i \ar[dr]_-f & X \ar[d]^-g \\ & S } \]

Assume \(X\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(N\), and that \(Y\) is, fibre by fibre, of dimension \(\leqslant d\). Let \(c=N-d\).

  1. One has \(\mathsf{R}^p i^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(p<2 c\); similarly for \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) replaced by a sheaf \(g^* \mathscr{F}\).

  2. If, above a dense open set \(U\) of \(S\), \(Y\) is, fibre by fibre, of dimension \(<d\), one has \(\mathsf{R}^p i^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(p\leqslant 2 c\). If moreover the complement \(Z\) of \(U\) does not locally disconnect \(S\), one has \(\mathsf{R}^pi^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(p\leqslant 2 c+1\).

Since \(\mathsf{R} g^! \mathscr{F}=g^*\mathscr{F}(N)[2N]\), the transitivity formula \(\mathsf{R} i^!\mathsf{R} g^!=\mathsf{R} f^!\) shows that \(\mathsf{R}^{2 c+q} i^!(g^*\mathscr{F})=0\Leftrightarrow \mathsf{R}^{-2 d+q}f^!(\mathscr{F})\). This reduces us to studying \(f\), i.e. to assuming that \(X=S\). Assertion (i) is then [2].
Let \(Y'\) be the inverse image of \(Z\) in \(Y\):
\[ \xymatrix{ Y' \ar[r]^-v \ar[d]^-f & Y \ar[d]^-f \\ Z \ar[r]^-u & S } \]

By (i), the \(\mathsf{R}^p f^! \mathbb{Z}/n\) are supported in \(Y'\) for \(p\leqslant -2 d+1\); and the spectral sequence \(\mathsf{R}^a v^!\mathsf{R}^b f^! \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{a+b} (f v)^!\) shows that they coincide with the \(\mathsf{R}^p(f v)^!\mathbb{Z}/n=\mathsf{R}^p(u f)^!\mathbb{Z}/n\). Applying (i) to \(Y'/Z\) and to the spectral sequence \(\mathsf{R}^a f^!\mathsf{R}^b u^! \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{a+b} (u f)^!\), we find that (ii) follows from the vanishing of \(\mathsf{R}^b u^! \mathbb{Z}/n\) for \(b=0\), or \(b=0\) and \(1\) as the case may be.

Grothendieck conjectures the following absolute analogue of 2.2.8 (semi-purity conjecture – a consequence of the purity conjecture): for \(Y\) of codimension \(\geqslant c\) in a regular \(X\), we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^i(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)=0\) for \(i<2 c\), at least if \(X\) is excellent.

We are now in a position to define the class of a cycle \(Y\) of codimension \(c\) in \(X\) smooth over a field \(k\). We write \(Y=\sum d_i Y_i\), where the \(Y_i\) are reduced and irreducible. An open subset \(U_i\) of \(Y_i\), whose complement has codimension \(>c\), is then a local complete intersection in \(X\). This makes it possible to define the local fundamental class of \(U_i\). By 2.2.6 and 2.2.8, this comes from a unique fundamental class \(\operatorname{cl}(Y_i)\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{Y_i}^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\), and we set
\[ \operatorname{cl}(Y) = \sum d_i \operatorname{cl}(Y_i) \in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{|Y|}^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \text{.} \]

In complex analytic geometry, a construction of Baum, Fulton and Mac Pherson [4] makes it possible to define, without restriction, the cohomology class of a local complete intersection \(Y\subset X\). Suppose \(Y\) purely of codimension \(c\), and let \(\mathscr{N}\) be the vector bundle on \(Y\), the normal bundle of \(Y\) in \(X\). Its local sections are those of \((\mathscr{I}/\mathscr{I}^2)^\vee\), where \(\mathscr{I}\) is the ideal sheaf of \(Y\). Recall that the sheaf of \(C^\infty\) functions on \(X\) is defined locally, in terms of local embeddings of \(X\) in \(\mathbb{C}^n\), as the restriction to \(X\) of the quotient of the sheaf of \(C^\infty\) functions on \(\mathbb{C}^n\) by the ideal generated by the real and imaginary parts of the equations defining \(X\). The bundle \(\mathscr{N}\) extends to a complex vector bundle \(C^\infty N\) on a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(Y\) in \(X\), and for \(U\) small enough, there exist sections \(f\) of \(N\), with zero locus \(Y\), and such that, on \(Y\), \(d f:\mathscr{N}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} N\) is the identity. Two choices of \(N\) and \(f\) are homotopic over a small enough \(Y\).

The cohomology class \(\operatorname{cl}(U)\) of the section \(0\) of \(N\) (denoted \(z:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} N\)) is defined: \(U\) is a local complete intersection in \(N\), and \(\mathsf{R}^i z^!\mathbb{Z} = 0\) for \(i\ne 2 c\), \(\mathsf{R}^{2 c} z^!\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}\). We have \(f^*:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_U^\bullet(N,\mathbb{Z}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z})\) and we set
\[ \operatorname{cl}(Y) = f^*\operatorname{cl}(U) \text{.} \]

The same construction works whenever one has, on an analytic subspace \(Y\) of \(X\), the following normal structure: a locally free sheaf \(\mathscr{C}\) of rank \(c\) on \(Y_\text{red}\), and an epimorphism \(\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{I}/\mathscr{I}\cdot \mathscr{I}_\text{red}\).
2.3 The homological method
Let \(f:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be a flat morphism of finite type, with fibres of dimension \(\leqslant d\). In [2], we defined a trace morphism
\[ \tag{2.3.1.1} \operatorname{tr}_f:\mathsf{R}^{2 d} f_! \mathbb{Z}/n(d) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n \text{.} \]

We have \(\mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)=0\) for \(i>2 d\), and \(\mathsf{R}^i f^!\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(i<-2 d\). This, together with the adjunction between \(\mathsf{R} f_!\) and \(\mathsf{R} f^!\), yields isomorphisms

\[ \tag{2.1.3.2} \begin{aligned} \hom\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 d}f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d),\mathbb{Z}/n\right) &= \hom\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d),\mathbb{Z}/n[-2 d]\right) \\ &= \hom\left(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathsf{R} f^!\mathbb{Z}/n(-d)[-2 d]\right) \\ &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(Y,\mathsf{R}^{-2 d}f^!\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \text{.} \end{aligned} \]
At least when \(S\) is a point, the image of \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) in the last two groups deserves the name of fundamental class of \(Y\) (in homology).
We again denote by \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) the image of \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) in the second group, and the morphisms deduced from it by functoriality. For example, for \(Y/S\) proper, the morphism

\[ \tag{2.3.1.3} \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\left(Y,\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\right) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\left(S,\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\right) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{i-2 d}(S,\mathbb{Z}/n) . } \]
Suppose \(Y\) contained in \(X\) smooth over \(S\), purely of relative dimension \(N\), and set \(c=N-d\).
\[ \xymatrix{ Y \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-i \ar[dr]_-f & X \ar[d] \\ & S } \]

We have \(\mathsf{R} f^! = \mathsf{R} i^!\mathsf{R} g^!\), and \(\mathsf{R} g^! \mathbb{Z}/n=\mathbb{Z}/n(-N)[-2 N]\). The fundamental class of \(Y\) is identified with an element of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(Y,\mathsf{R} i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(c)[2 c]\right)=\underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\), the class \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\) of \(Y\) in \(X\). We shall see later that it depends only on \(Y\subset X\), not on the projection of \(X\) onto \(S\), and that for \(Y\) a local complete intersection, it induces the local class of the preceding number.
Let us make explicit the isomorphism
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} \hom\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 d}f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d),\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \]
which transforms \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\) into \(\operatorname{tr}_f\): via the isomorphisms

\begin{align*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(\mathsf{R} i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \\ &= \hom_Y\left(\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d],\mathsf{R} i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(N)[2 N]\right) \\ &= \hom_X\left(\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d]_Y,\mathbb{Z}/n(N)[2 N]\right) \text{,} \end{align*}
it is the top row of

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c} \ar[r] \ar[dr]_-{(3)} & \hom\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d],\mathsf{R} f_! \mathsf{R} i^!\mathbb{Z}/n(N)[2 N]\right) \ar[r]^-{(1)} \ar[d]^-{\operatorname{tr}_i} \ar@{}[dr]|-{(2)} & \hom\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2d],\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \ar@{=}[d] \\ & \hom\left(\mathsf{R} g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d]_Y,\mathsf{R} g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(N)[2 N]\right) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{tr}_g} & \hom\left(\mathsf{R} g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d]_Y,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) , } \]

where (1) is the adjunction arrow \(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathsf{R} f^!\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \text{id}\). The commutativity (2) expresses that the isomorphism \(\mathsf{R} f^!=\mathsf{R} i^!\mathsf{R} g^!\) is defined by adjunction. Finally, the arrow deduced from (3)

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \otimes \mathsf{R}^{2 d} g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}^{2 N} g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(N) \]
is interpreted as a cup-product (cf. 1.2).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.3.2

The class \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\in\underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\) has the characteristic property that, for every local section \(u\) of \(\mathsf{R}^{2 d}f_! \mathbb{Z}/n(d)\), we have

\[ \operatorname{tr}_f(u) = \operatorname{tr}_g\left(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\smallsmile u\right) \text{.} \]

From the fact that \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\) already has an image \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) in \(\hom\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d],\mathbb{Z}/n\right)\), formula 2.3.2 holds for the arrows deduced from \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) by functoriality. For example, for \(X\) proper over \(S\) and \(u\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y,\mathbb{Z}/n)\), the formula holds in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(S,\mathbb{Z}/n(-d)\right)\). For \(v\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\), it gives
\[ \operatorname{tr}_f(i^* v) = \operatorname{tr}_g\left(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\smallsmile v\right) \text{,} \]
where the cup-product can be computed in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\).
We shall define the trace morphisms, and hence the class \(\operatorname{cl}(Y)\), under more general hypotheses. So consider a diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ Y \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[dr]_-f & X \ar[d]^-g \\ & S } \]

with \(g\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(N\), and \(Y\) closed in \(X\), fibre by fibre of dimension \(\leqslant d\). We further endow \(Y\) with a “weight” \(\mathscr{K}\) of the following type: \(\mathscr{K}\in\mathsf{D}_{\text{parf},X}^b\) is a bounded complex of sheaves of \(\mathscr{O}\)-modules on \(X\), of finite \(\operatorname{Tor}\)-dimension over \(S\) (or over \(X\), it amounts to the same thing) and whose cohomology sheaves are coherent and supported in \(Y\). We propose to define a morphism \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}:\mathsf{R}^{2 d}f_! \mathbb{Z}/n(d) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\). For \(Y\) flat over \(S\) and \(\mathscr{K}=\mathscr{O}_Y\), this will be the previous trace morphism. In general, it depends only on the lengths of \(\mathscr{K}\) at the generic points \(y\) of the irreducible components of \(Y(\operatorname{lg}_y(\mathscr{K}) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{lg} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathscr{K})_y)\).
Finally, we shall denote by \(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K})\) the class supported in \(Y\) such that
\[ \tag{2.3.3.1} \operatorname{tr}_g\left(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K})\smallsmile u\right) = \operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}(u) \text{.} \]
The construction of \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}\) is parallel to that of [2]; we shall indicate only the main lines.

\(d=0\) (\(f\) quasi-finite). Let \(x\) be a geometric point of \(Y\), \(s\) its image in \(S\), \(\mathscr{K}_{(x)}\) the inverse image of \(\mathscr{K}\) on the strict localization of \(X\) at \(x\), \(\mathscr{K}_{(x)s} = \mathscr{K}_{(x)}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathscr{O}_{S,s}^h} k(s)\) its inverse image on the geometric fibre at \(s\), and \(n(x)=\sum (-1)^i \dim_{k(s)} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathscr{K}_{(x)s})\). The function \(x\mapsto n(x)\) is a weighting of \(f\), and we take the corresponding trace morphism [2]. The formation of the weighting \(n(x)\), and of \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}\), is compatible with any base change.

General case. If \(u:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_S^d\) is such that \(u i\) is quasi-finite, we set \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}} = \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{A}_S^d}\circ \operatorname{tr}_{u i,\mathscr{K}}\). This trace morphism is clearly compatible with any base change \(S'/S\). To prove that it does not depend on \(u\), we may therefore suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\). In this case, let \(Y_i\) be the irreducible components of \(Y\), and \(\operatorname{lg}_i\) the length of \(\mathscr{K}\) at the generic point of \(Y_i\). If \(\alpha_i\) is the inclusion of \((Y_i)_\text{red}\) in \(Y\), we have
\[ \tag{2.3.4} \operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}} = \sum \operatorname{lg}_i \operatorname{tr}_{Y_{i,\text{red}/S}} \alpha_i^\ast \]
(this formula follows from the analogous and easy formula for \(\operatorname{tr}_{u i}\)).
This defines \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}\) locally on \(Y\); we then proceed as in [2].

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.5

If \(g=g'g'':X\xrightarrow{g''} S'\xrightarrow{g'} S\), with \(g'\) and \(g''\) smooth and purely of relative dimension \(N'\) and \(N''\), and if \(Y\) is again, over \(S'\), fibre by fibre of codimension \(\geqslant c\), then the class \(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K})\) is the same, computed in terms of \(g\) or of \(g''\).
Let \(f'=g'' i\) and \(d'=d-N'\). The formula \(\operatorname{tr}_g=\operatorname{tr}_{g'}\operatorname{tr}_{g''}\) ([2] Var 3) ensures the commutativity of

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_X^{2 c}\left(Z,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right) \ar[d] \\ \hom_{S'}\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d')[2 d'],\mathsf{R} g_!''\mathbb{Z}/n(N'')[2 N'']\right) \ar[r] \ar[d]^-{\mathsf{R} g_!'(N')} & \hom_{S'}\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 d'} f_!' \mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \ar[d]^-{\operatorname{tr}_{g'}\circ \mathsf{R}^{2 N'} g_!'} \\ \hom_S\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2d],\mathsf{R} g_!'\mathbb{Z}/n(N)[2 N]\right) \ar[r] & \hom_S\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 d} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) } \]

while the analogous formula, easy to verify, \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}=\operatorname{tr}_{g'}\operatorname{tr}_{f',\mathscr{K}}\) ensures that the image of \(\operatorname{tr}_{f',\mathscr{K}}\) is \(\operatorname{tr}_{f,\mathscr{K}}\). The assertion follows.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.6

If \(Y\) is a divisor in \(X\), the class 2.3.2 coincides with the class 2.1.2.

By semi-purity (2.2.6(i) and 2.2.8(i)), the problem is local on \(Y\); using 2.3.5 to replace \(S\) by a suitable \(S'\), this allows us to suppose that \(N=1\). Using the semi-purity again (2.2.6(ii) and 2.2.8(ii)), it suffices to prove 2.3.6 over the generic points of \(S\). An étale localization then reduces us to supposing \(S\) the spectrum of a algebraically closed field \(k\). The classes 2.3.2 and 2.1.2 each being additive in \(Y\), this reduces us to the case where \(Y\) is a closed point on a smooth curve over \(k\). That the characteristic property 2.3.2 is satisfied is then the fundamental compatibility 2.1.5.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.7

The formation of \(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K})\) is compatible with any base change \(S'/S\).
This follows from the same assertion for the trace morphisms.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.3.8

(i) \(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K})\) depends only on \(Y\subset X\) and on the lengths of \(\mathscr{K}\) at the generic points of \(Y\). This class is additive in \(\mathscr{K}\). For \(\mathscr{K}=\mathscr{O}_Y\) and \(Y\) a local complete intersection, it induces the local class 2.2.2.

(ii) Let there be a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[r]^-u \ar[d] & X \ar[d] \\ S' \ar[r] & S } \]

with \(X'\) smooth over \(S'\). If \(u^{-1}(Y)\) is again fibre by fibre of codimension \(\geqslant c\), then

\[ \operatorname{cl}\left(u^{-1}(Y),\mathsf{L} u^\ast\mathscr{K}\right) = u^\ast \operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K}) \text{.} \]

(iii) Let \(Y'\subset X\) be fibre by fibre of codimension \(\geqslant c'\), \(\mathscr{K}'\) a weight on \(Y'\), and suppose that \(Y\cap Y'\) is fibre by fibre of codimension \(\geqslant c+c'\). Then

\[ \operatorname{cl}\left(Y\cap Y',\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K}'\right) = \operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K}) \smallsmile \operatorname{cl}(Y',\mathscr{K}') \text{.} \]

Given \(Y\subset X/S\) as stated, it follows from semi-purity (2.2.6, 2.2.8) that to verify that two classes in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_Y^{2 c}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c)\right)\) coincide, it suffices to verify it locally at the generic points of \(Y\), or even, after any base change \(s\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) (\(s\) a generic geometric point of \(S\)), at the generic points of \(Y\).
(B) Proof of (ii) for \(S=S'\) and \(u\) a closed embedding

By the localization (A), we may suppose that \(X'\) is the inverse image of the section \(0\) under a smooth morphism \(v:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_S^{N'}\)
\[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[r]^-u \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^-v \\ S \ar[r]^-0 & \mathbb{A}_S^{N'} \ar[r]^-\pi & S } \]
We apply 2.3.5 to \(g=\pi v\) and 2.3.7 to the change of base \(S\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_S^{N'}\).
(C) In a product situation:

\(X=X'\times_S X''\), \(Y=Y'\times_S Y''\), \(\mathscr{K}=\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_S \mathscr{K}''\), we have \(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K}) = \operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K}')\smallsmile \operatorname{cl}(Y'',\mathscr{K}'')\) (external cup-product, i.e. \(\operatorname{pr}_1^\ast \operatorname{cl}(Y',\mathscr{K}')\smallsmile \operatorname{pr}_2^\ast \operatorname{cl}(Y'',\mathscr{K}'')\)).
From the functorial properties of \(\operatorname{tr}_g\) [2] follows the commutativity of

\[ \xymatrix@=0.5cm{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{X'}^{2c'}\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_{X''}^{2 c''}\ar[r] \ar[d] & \hom_S\left(\mathsf{R} f_!' \mathbb{Z}/n(d')[2 d'],\mathsf{R} g_!'\mathbb{Z}/n(N')[2 N']\right)\otimes \cdots \ar[r] \ar[d] & \hom_S\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 d'} f_!' \mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \otimes \cdots \ar[d] \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_X^{2 c} \ar[r] & \hom_S\left(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2 d],\mathsf{R} g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(N)[2 N]\right) \ar[r] & \hom_S\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 d}f_!\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) } \]
and we verify that \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) is the image of \(\operatorname{tr}_{f'}\otimes \operatorname{tr}_{f''}\), whence the assertion.
Proof of (ii)
(2.3.7) and a preliminary base change reduce us to supposing that \(S=S'\). Let us factor \(u\) through its graph:
\[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[r]^-{(\text{id},u)} & X'\times X \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{pr}_2} & X . } \]

This leads us to treat separately \(\operatorname{pr}_2\), which comes under (C) for \(X'=X'\), \(\mathscr{K}'=\mathscr{O}_{x'}\) (with \(\operatorname{cl}(Y')=1\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\)), and \((\text{id},u)\), which comes under (B).
Proof of (iii)

Let \(\delta:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\times_S X\) be the diagonal inclusion. We use the formula \(\delta^\ast(Y_1\times_S Y_2) = Y_1\cap Y_2\) to reduce to (B) and (C).
Proof of (i)

The base change \(S_\text{red}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) replaces \(X\) by \(X_\text{red}\); this reduces us to supposing \(X\) and \(S\) reduced. A localization in the neighbourhood of the generic points of \(Y\) then reduces us to the case where \(Y_\text{red}\) is irreducible and the complete intersection of \(c\) divisors \(D_i\). The same localization, and the definition of \(\operatorname{tr}\) in the quasi-finite case, then show that \(\operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K})=\operatorname{lg}\operatorname{cl}(Y_\text{red},\mathscr{O}_{Y_\text{red}})\), where \(\operatorname{lg}\) is the length of \(\mathscr{K}\) at the generic point of \(Y\). By (iv), we therefore have
\[ \operatorname{cl}(Y,\mathscr{K}) = \operatorname{lg} \prod_i \operatorname{cl}(D_i,\mathscr{O}_{D_i}) \]
and we conclude by 2.3.6.
For \(S\) the spectrum of a field, and the class of a cycle being defined as in 2.2.10, assertion (iii) says that, if two cycles \(Y'\) and \(Y''\) meet in the right dimension, then
\[ \operatorname{cl}(Y'\cap Y'') = \operatorname{cl}(Y')\smallsmile \operatorname{cl}(Y'')\text{,} \]
provided that the multiplicities of the components of \(Y'\cap Y''\) are computed as alternating sums of \(\operatorname{Tor}\).

Let \(X/\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) algebraically closed. If two cycles of codimension \(c\) in \(X\) are algebraically equivalent, it follows from the existence of the relative theory above that the images in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 c}(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c))\) of their classes are the fibres, at two points of a suitable connected \(S\), of a section over \(S\) of the constant sheaf \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 c}(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c))\) (the sheaf \(\mathsf{R}^{2 c} f_\ast \mathbb{Z}/n(c)\) for \(f=\operatorname{pr}_2:X\times S\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\)): two algebraically equivalent cycles have the same class in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 c}(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(c))\).

pages.title: Application: the Lefschetz trace formula in the proper and smooth case

blocks.html: 3 Application: the Lefschetz trace formula in the proper and smooth case

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be proper and smooth algebraic varieties over a algebraically closed field \(k\), purely of dimensions \(N\) and \(M\). Via the Künneth isomorphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X\times Y)=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)\), the trace morphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X\times Y)(M)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\) is none other than \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\otimes (\)the trace morphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)(M)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Q}_\ell)\). The morphism being homogeneous of even degree, there is no problem of sign. We denote it by \(\int_Y\).

A class \(\eta\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 q}(X\times Y)(q)\) defines a morphism of degree \(2(q-N)\) \(\eta_{XY}:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)(N-q)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\), by the formula
\[ \beta \mapsto \int_Y \eta\cdot \operatorname{pr}_2^\ast \beta \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3

Let \(p\) and \(q\) be two integers, with \(p+q=N+M\), and \(\varepsilon\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 p}(X\times Y)(p)\), \(\eta\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 q}(X\times Y)(q)\). The trace of \(\eta_{X Y}\varepsilon_{Y X}:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\) being understood in the sense of 1.3, we then have

\[ \operatorname{tr}_{X\times Y}(\eta\cdot \varepsilon) = \operatorname{tr}\left(\eta_{X Y}\varepsilon_{Y X},\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\right) \text{.} \]

To exorcise the signs, it is convenient to keep, from the grading of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\), only the underlying \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-grading. To avoid carrying the Tate twists around, we further fix an isomorphism \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell(1)=\mathbb{Q}_\ell\). Let \(\alpha_Y\) be the homomorphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)^\vee\) (an isomorphism) making commutative the diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y) \ar[r] \ar[d]^-{\alpha_Y\otimes 1} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{tr}} & \mathbb{Q}_\ell \ar@{=}[d] \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)^\vee \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y) \ar[rr]^-{\text{(1.3.1)}} & & \mathbb{Q}_\ell . } \]
The map \(\eta_{X Y}\) is the image of \(\eta\) under

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X\times Y) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y) \ar[r]^-{\alpha_Y} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X) \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y)^\vee \ar@{=}[r]^-{\text{(1.3.2)}} & \hom\left(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y),\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\right) , } \]
and similarly for \(\varepsilon\). The definition 1.3.4 of the trace then reduces 3.3 to the formula \(\operatorname{tr}_{X\times Y}=\operatorname{tr}_X\otimes \operatorname{tr}_Y\).
3.4 Remark

The proof of 3.3 does not use that \(\alpha_X\) and \(\alpha_Y\) are isomorphisms. It holds without supposing \(X\) and \(Y\) smooth. However, outside the smooth case, it is difficult to find cohomology classes to which one would want to apply 3.3.
3.5 Remark

If \(\varepsilon,\eta\) are the cohomology classes of algebraic cycles \(A\) and \(B\) on \(X\times Y\), of codimension \(p\) and \(q\), and \(A\cap B\) is of dimension \(0\), then \(\operatorname{tr}_{X\times Y}(\eta\varepsilon)\) is the intersection multiplicity \(A\cdot B\), computed by an alternating sum of \(\operatorname{Tor}\) (2.3.9).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6

For \(q=M\) and \(\eta=\operatorname{cl}(B)\) the class of a subscheme \(B\subset X\times Y\), finite over \(X\), the map \(\eta_{X Y}\) is the composite

\[ \xymatrix{ \eta_{X Y} : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{pr}_2^\ast} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(B) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{tr}_{B/X}} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X) . } \]
By 3.2 and (2.3.3.1) for \(\mathscr{K}=\mathscr{O}_B\), we indeed have

\[ \eta_{X Y}(\beta) = \operatorname{tr}_{X\times Y/X}\left(\operatorname{cl}(B)\cdot \operatorname{pr}_2^\ast\beta\right) = \operatorname{tr}_{B/X}\left(\operatorname{pr}_2^\ast \beta\right) \text{.} \]
The most important case is that where \(B\) is the graph of a map \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\). In this case, 3.6 shows that \(\eta_{X Y}=f^\ast\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.7

Let \(f\) be an endomorphism of \(X\), proper and smooth over an algebraically closed field \(k\). Suppose that the fixed points of \(f\) are isolated. Then, the trace \(\sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X))\) is the number of fixed points of \(f\), each counted with its multiplicity.
In 3.5, we take \(A=\)graph of the identity, \(B=\)graph of \(f\), and we apply 3.3, 3.6.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.8

Let \(X\) be a curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), obtained by extension of the scalars from \(X_0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(f\) the Frobenius morphism. Then, \(\sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X)\right)\) is the number of fixed points of \(f\).

We may replace \(X\) by \(X_\text{red}\), hence suppose \(X\) reduced. Let \(U\) be the open subset of \(X\) where \(X\) is smooth of dimension \(1\), and \(\overline{U}\) the projective and smooth completion of \(U\). The long exact cohomology sequences for \((X,U)\) and \((\overline{U},U)\) give

\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X)\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(U)\right) + \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X\setminus U)\right) \]
and

\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\overline{U})\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(U)\right) + \operatorname{tr}\left(f^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\overline{U}\setminus U)\right) \text{.} \]

The same formulas hold for the numbers of fixed points. The formula 3.8 being clear for a scheme of dimension \(0\), this reduces to proving 3.8 for \(\overline{U}\). This case comes under 3.7. The fact that \(d f=0\) guarantees that the fixed points are all of multiplicity one.
3.9 Remark

For \(X\) of dimension \(\leqslant 1\) over \(k\) algebraically closed, and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) such that \(d f=0\), it is not difficult to verify that 3.8 is still valid.
